record.paper_title: Quantum Communication: From Fundamentals to Recent Trends, Challenges and Open Problems
record.context_brief: quantum repeater memories and multi-photon generation
record.original_question: How can quantum repeaters improve quantum-state coherence time, improve the efficiency of on-demand state retrieval, and support deterministic generation of multi-photon quantum states required by encoded repeater techniques?

evidence.quote: Storage and on-demand retrieval of a photon’s quantum state with low efficiency are shown in [213], [214], [215], [216] using heralded quantum memory. Research is going on to increase the coherence time of quantum states and increase the efficiency of on-demand state retrieval.

This technique achieves a high communication rate, however, one limitation here is that this mechanism requires deterministic generation of multi-photons quantum state, which is far from implementation till now [221].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A quantum repeater is a device used to extend the range of quantum communication by dividing a long channel into shorter elementary links, generating entanglement on each link, storing it in quantum memories, and then performing entanglement swapping between adjacent links. A heralded quantum memory is a physical system that, upon a successful heralding signal, stores the quantum state of an incoming photon and allows on-demand retrieval (re-emission) of that photon at a later time, with retrieval efficiency η and coherence (storage) time τ. Encoded quantum repeater schemes are protocols in which logical qubits are encoded across multiple photons (using quantum error-correcting codes), and these protocols require the deterministic generation of multi-photon entangled states (such as GHZ, cluster, or tree-graph states of a prescribed size n ≥ 3) on demand and with success probability arbitrarily close to 1.

Provide concrete physical and protocol-level designs of quantum repeaters that simultaneously achieve all of the following goals:

(1) Quantum memories whose coherence time τ is long enough relative to the elementary-link entanglement generation time so that end-to-end entanglement distribution rates over continental distances become practical.

(2) High on-demand retrieval efficiency η of stored single-photon quantum states (ideally η → 1) from heralded quantum memories.

(3) Sources or mechanisms that deterministically generate the multi-photon entangled states (of arbitrary specified graph structure and size) required by encoded quantum repeater architectures, with near-unit success probability per generation cycle.

Determine whether such repeaters can be constructed and, if so, give explicit constructions or quantitative bounds on the achievable parameters (τ, η, success probability of n-photon state generation) under realistic noise and loss models.
artifact.status_search_result: Increasing quantum-memory coherence time, raising on-demand retrieval efficiency, and achieving deterministic multi-photon entangled state generation remain active open research problems in quantum repeater development. Recent (2024–2026) experimental and theoretical work continues to push individual parameters (e.g., second-scale coherence in rare-earth-ion memories, improved cluster-state generation from quantum dots), but no system to date jointly satisfies all three requirements at the levels needed for encoded repeater protocols.
